The Children's Peace Monument in Hiroshima, Japan, commemorates Sadako Sasaki and thousands of child victims of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima. The monument is dedicated to peace and is located in Hiroshima. 

The development of nuclear weapons began with scientific breakthroughs in the 1930s, leading to the Manhattan Project, a collaboration between the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada during World War II. The project aimed to counter the suspected Nazi German atomic bomb project. In August 1945, two fission bombs were dropped on Japan, marking the only use of nuclear weapons in combat to date.

Jacob Beser, a lieutenant in the United States Army Air Forces, served as a radar specialist aboard the "Enola Gay" when it dropped the Little Boy atomic bomb on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945. Three days later, Beser was a crew member aboard "Bockscar" when the Fat Man bomb was dropped on Nagasaki. He is the only person to have served as a strike crew member of both 1945 atomic bomb missions.

Rear Admiral William Sterling Parsons, an American naval officer, worked as an ordnance expert on the Manhattan Project during World War II. Parsons was the weaponeer on the "Enola Gay" and decided to arm the bomb in flight to avoid a nuclear explosion if the aircraft crashed and burned on takeoff. He inserted the powder charge and detonator into the bomb while the aircraft was en route to Hiroshima.

The People's Republic of China initiated the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" project, which involved the development of atomic and hydrogen bombs, as well as artificial satellites. China tested its first atomic bomb in 1964 and its first hydrogen bomb in 1967. The country successfully launched its first satellite, DFH-1, in 1970.

The book "Hiroshima" by John Hersey tells the stories of six survivors of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima, covering a period of time immediately prior to and one year after the atomic bomb was dropped on August 6, 1945. The book was originally published in "The New Yorker" and is regarded as one of the earliest examples of New Journalism.

The "Fat Man" was the codename for the atomic bomb detonated over Nagasaki on August 9, 1945. It was built by scientists and engineers at Los Alamos Laboratory using plutonium from the Hanford Site and dropped from the Boeing B-29 Superfortress "Bockscar". 

Morris R. Jeppson served as assistant weaponeer on the "Enola Gay", which dropped the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945. 

"Little Boy" was the codename for the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945. It was the first atomic bomb used in warfare and exploded with an energy of approximately 15 kton TNT.

Vice Admiral Frederick Lincoln Ashworth served as the weaponeer on the B-29 "Bockscar" that dropped a Fat Man atomic bomb on Nagasaki, Japan, on August 9, 1945.
